scenes.text: So, why is staying in sport harder than starting? Two puzzles. First, a story. Some kids play in a park every afternoon, just because they enjoy it. An adult starts paying them a little each time. A few weeks later the payments stop, and the kids stop coming, and they now play less than before any money was involved. Second, a seventeen-year-old has played representative sport since she was eight. Everyone calls her an athlete. She tears a knee ligament, is out for a year, and copes far worse than a teammate with the same injury. Is that really about the knee?

Start with personal identity: your sense of who you are, built from the roles and groups you treat as defining. People tend to act like the person they believe they are. Compare two sentences. I want to get fitter is an intention, and it often loses to a cold morning. I'm someone who runs is an identity, and it holds up far better. Identity works on sport in three ways. It decides whether you start, because people join where they can picture themselves belonging, so who already plays sends a signal. It decides whether you keep going. A bad session tells a committed player this happens to people like me, and tells a newcomer she was right to doubt. Same session, opposite conclusions. And it shapes performance. If your worth rides on the result, an ordinary game becomes a test of you, and that pressure can drag attention onto the movement.

Now the seventeen-year-old. A strong athletic identity, how much you see yourself as an athlete, is genuinely useful. It drives commitment and persistence. The risk comes when it's the only identity. That's identity foreclosure: committing so fully to one role that others never develop. Her injury hasn't just taken a season. It's taken her answer to who she is. The protection isn't caring less. It's having other identities that are real too, so a lost season is a serious loss, not a total one. And talking it through with someone she trusts helps.

Next, motivation: what you choose to do, and how hard you go at it. Intrinsic motivation comes from the activity itself: enjoyment, interest, getting better. Extrinsic motivation comes from something separate: a medal, selection, money or praise. Both work. The difference is how long they last. Ask one question: what happens when the person stops winning? Extrinsic motivation lasts as long as the reward. Intrinsic lasts as long as the activity. Now the park. Paying for something the kids already enjoyed changed why they were there. Play became a job. When the money stopped, the new reason had gone, and the old one had been pushed out. That's the overjustification effect. Not every reward does this. A reward that shows real improvement can build motivation. A reward that controls, do this to get that, crowds it out.

There's a second, separate axis. Positive motivation chases something good, like a faster time. Negative motivation avoids something bad, like being dropped. Every reason has an answer on both axes, so there are four kinds, not two. I love it when a move finally works is intrinsic and positive, the most durable. If I miss training, the coach will drop me is extrinsic and negative, the most fragile. Negative motivation does work in the short term. But it's stressful, it makes players play safe instead of trying hard things, and it isn't fun, so it speeds up dropping out.

So how does a coach grow the durable kind? Intrinsic motivation grows where three needs are met, and a coach controls each one. Competence: feeling capable and improving. Give challenges they can reach, and compare them with their own past, not with a ranking. Autonomy: feeling you chose this. Offer real choices, and give reasons instead of orders. Relatedness: feeling you belong and matter here. Learn names, give everyone a role, and build a group that would notice someone missing. Earlier, you saw a session aimed at the fittest player shut everyone else out. That's competence denied. And relatedness is often the cheapest need to meet.

So what has all this got to do with performance? The pressure of a big moment is real. But the larger effects are quieter. Motivated players practise with attention, and earlier, you saw that attentive practice, not time served, moves a learner through the stages. And above all, they keep playing. The biggest effect of psychology on performance is often simply this: still playing at seventeen, instead of stopping at thirteen.
Two things to remember. Ask what happens when they stop winning. And grow motivation with competence, autonomy and belonging.

Two exam questions. First. A swimmer gives three reasons for training. One: I love how the water feels when I'm swimming well. Two: I don't want my parents to think the fees were wasted. Three: I want to make the state team. Classify each reason on both motivation axes. Pause here to answer.

One is intrinsic and positive: the feel of swimming well is the activity itself, and she's chasing it. Two is extrinsic and negative: she's avoiding her parents' disappointment. Three is extrinsic and positive: she's chasing selection. The classic mistake is calling reason three intrinsic, just because she wants it so much.

Second. A coach posts every player's weekly fitness test result, ranked from first to last, on the changing-room wall. Explain how this is likely to affect participation, using the needs that support intrinsic motivation, and propose a better alternative. Pause here to answer.

A public ranking compares players with each other, not with their own past. Those near the bottom feel less competent every week, even when they're improving, and public last place weakens belonging. So they're the likeliest to drop out. Instead, show each player their own progress privately, and celebrate personal bests. The classic mistake is assuming a ranking motivates everyone.

So, for any player, ask who they think they are, which kind of motivation is carrying them, and which need is going hungry. But even a well-motivated person can mean to train three times a week, and not do it. Why don't good intentions turn into exercise?
